expectations.text: Answers no: marketplace-facilitator and deemed-supplier obligations can attach to the platform by law regardless of who bills the customer
expectations.evidence: "Short answer: no, not entirely... Facilitator and deemed-supplier rules attach by law, not by billing posture."

expectations.text: Names US marketplace-facilitator statutes and ties them to the 2018 South Dakota v. Wayfair economic-nexus decision
expectations.evidence: "US marketplace-facilitator statutes exist in most sales-tax states (since *Wayfair*)"

expectations.text: States the US facilitator framework is state-by-state rather than federal, with variations such as excluded local taxes or continuing seller informational returns
expectations.evidence: "depends on each state's definition of 'facilitator'. Some key on payment processing, some on listing plus other criteria... counsel has to check each one."

expectations.text: Names the EU deemed-supplier rule (Article 14a of the e-commerce VAT package, in force since 1 July 2021) treating the electronic interface as having bought and resold the supply
expectations.evidence: Only "The EU deemed-supplier rule targets B2C supplies." No Article 14a, date or mechanism.

expectations.text: States the EU deemed-supplier rule attaches to B2C supplies specifically, making the individual-buyer share a tax-design input rather than demographic trivia
expectations.evidence: "The 12% of seats bought by individuals changes the EU picture. The EU deemed-supplier rule targets B2C supplies."

expectations.text: Notes B2B cross-border EU supplies are typically reverse-charged to the business buyer, so the business-buyer portion is a lighter version of the layer, not an exemption
expectations.evidence: "B2B cross-border VAT is normally reverse-charged"; table: "Vendor, reverse charge | Lighter".

expectations.text: Rejects the single blanket clause that vendors are responsible for all taxes as the deliverable
expectations.evidence: "a one-line 'vendors are responsible for all taxes' clause hides the parts that matter"; the deliverable is a split plus companion clauses.

expectations.text: Specifies the deliverable as a published split naming which tax, which jurisdiction, and whose obligation, rather than a binary toggle
expectations.evidence: "The skill's rule is a published jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction split, never a single toggle." Followed by a table.

expectations.text: States that marketplace-facilitator or deemed-supplier status is tax law while merchant of record is card-network status, and that the two are legally distinct and do not always coincide
expectations.evidence: "Tax law and card-network merchant-of-record status are legally distinct and don't always coincide."

expectations.text: Warns that marketplace sales may still count toward a seller's own nexus thresholds or filing obligations even where a platform remits
expectations.evidence: No mention of seller nexus thresholds or filing obligations.

expectations.text: States this is not tax advice and routes the published split through qualified counsel before shipping
expectations.evidence: "Have counsel review the split... this is not tax advice."

expectations.text: Flags that collecting 12% from developer-reported figures means the platform learns its own revenue from the payer, and pairs it with an anti-circumvention rule backed by a delisting path
expectations.evidence: "You collect the 12% from vendor self-reports... An anti-circumvention rule with a delisting path. Without the delisting path it's only a preference."

expectations.text: Answers no: marketplace-facilitator and deemed-supplier obligations can attach to the platform by law regardless of who bills the customer
